transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thank you for, uh, fitting me in. I know I probably should have made this appointment a long time ago. It’s just... well, I’ve been a software developer for over two decades now, ever since grad school, and I’ve always had a lot on my plate. I used to be able to sort of... power through it, I guess? 

But what finally pushed me to come in today, what actually made me pick up the phone, is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. And there are so many moving parts right now. I’ve got these patent notes I’m supposed to be finalizing for a new algorithm I've been working on, and then I’m doing all the prep for this big developer workshop I agreed to run. Plus, my wife and I do this local arts thing, so we have these strict gallery deadlines coming up, and on top of all of that, I have all the daily team decisions I need to make at my actual job. It’s just... it’s a lot. 

And the real problem is, because I can’t seem to figure out how to structure or sequence any of it in my head, I just end up starting whatever is loudest, you know? Instead of tackling what actually matters or what’s most critical for my career, I just react to whoever is pinging me on Slack the most, or whatever email just came in with a red exclamation mark. It’s like I have fifty tabs open in my brain and they're all playing audio, and I'm just constantly putting out tiny, noisy fires while the important stuff gets completely ignored. I just don't know how to sort it all out anymore.
Were you having these kinds of attention and organization problems back when you were a child, before age 12?

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because... well, my wife and I were actually just talking about this not too long ago. When you're in the thick of it, you sort of think it's just a current problem, right? Like it's just the gallery deadlines and the patent notes overwhelming me. But... yeah, before age 12? Definitely. 

Looking back, this was absolutely there in grade school, too. I think third or fourth grade was when it really started becoming a constant, glaring issue. My mom actually kept a bunch of my old report cards in this big plastic storage bin in her attic, and we were looking through them a few years back. Every single one of them—and I mean literally almost every one from first grade all the way up—had the exact same comments written in the margins by my teachers. They would always write that I was a bright kid, you know, very capable of doing the work... but then there was always the caveat. It was always, "but he daydreams too much," or "he spends half the day staring out the window." I would just drift off into my own world, thinking about how a clock worked or whatever sci-fi book I was reading at the time, and I'd completely tune out the classroom. 

And the organization... oh man, it was a total disaster. I had these specific homework folders, you know, those glossy two-pocket ones? I lost them constantly. I’d leave them on the bus, or they'd just vanish into the void. But I think the most frustrating part—and this drove my parents absolutely up the wall—was that I would actually *do* the work. I would sit at the kitchen table, finish the spelling worksheet or whatever it was, put it in my bag... and then the next day, I just forgot to turn in the finished assignments. The teacher would call for them, and I'd either forget I even had it, or I couldn't find it in the absolute black hole that was my desk. I'd get a zero on something I had literally completed twelve hours prior. I remember one time in fifth grade, Mr. Peterson actually made me dump my entire desk out onto the floor, and sure enough, my missing math packet was just crumpled up in the very back under a dried-out glue stick. 

So, yeah, long before I was a teenager, I was already struggling with... well, with all of this. It’s like the fifty tabs were open back then, too, just with different labels on them.
Do you spend a lot of time feeling worried or on edge about many different things?

No, I wouldn't say I'm worried or on edge about many different things. I mean, I don't sit around chewing my fingernails about the state of the world or what might happen tomorrow. It’s not a generalized sense of dread, you know? Like, my wife, she’s a bit more of a worrier. She’ll fret over whether we left the stove on, or if the dog is acting weird because he ate something in the yard, or if she offended someone at the gallery by looking at them funny. But me? No, I don't have that kind of free-floating anxiety. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, I get stressed out when I realize I’ve dropped the ball on something, like when I suddenly remember a deadline for the workshop is in two hours and I haven't even opened the document. But that's just a reaction to the chaos, you know? It's not this constant, humming worry about everything under the sun. It's just... frustration, mostly. Frustration that I can't seem to get my ducks in a row. But as for feeling generally anxious or on edge about a bunch of different stuff? No, not really. I'm usually too busy trying to figure out which fire to put out first to have the energy to worry about things that haven't even caught fire yet.

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly inattentive type (ICD-10 F90.0): longstanding inattention, poor organization, losing items, failing to turn in completed work, and marked distractibility beginning in childhood before age 12 and continuing into adulthood with clear functional impact. Generalized anxiety disorder is less likely because he explicitly denies pervasive, free-floating worry or chronic on-edge anxiety. A residual inattentive presentation without full syndrome is a secondary consideration, but the history supports full ADHD criteria.
